question: What is DispatcherServlet in Spring MVC?
title: DispatcherServlet in Spring MVC — Front Controller Pattern
direct_answer: DispatcherServlet is Spring MVC's front controller servlet. It handles requests mapped to that servlet, finds a handler through HandlerMapping, invokes it through a HandlerAdapter, and coordinates body writing, view rendering, and exception resolution. It does not intercept literally every HTTP request: servlet mappings, filters, static-resource handling, and other servlets determine which requests reach it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring MVC request processing pipeline and the role of the front controller pattern
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking controllers directly handle HTTP requests — DispatcherServlet is the single entry point that orchestrates the entire request flow
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through the full request lifecycle: DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping → Controller → ViewResolver/MessageConverter → Response, mentioning each component's responsibility

sections.title: DispatcherServlet as Spring MVC's Front Controller
sections.content:
The main path is request -> filters -> DispatcherServlet -> HandlerMapping -> HandlerAdapter/controller -> response handling. HandlerExceptionResolvers can take over when invocation fails.

Spring Boot registers and configures the servlet when Spring MVC is present and the required conditions match. Traditional Spring applications can register it through servlet configuration. Understanding the collaborators is more useful than imagining DispatcherServlet as a large switch statement that directly calls controllers.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: It is one central entry point for the Spring MVC request pipeline.
HandlerMapping finds the matching handler; HandlerAdapter invokes it.
ViewResolvers, HttpMessageConverters, and HandlerExceptionResolvers handle different outcomes.
Spring Boot commonly maps it to /, subject to the application's servlet configuration.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For GET /orders/42, the servlet asks its handler mappings for a matching controller method, binds method arguments, invokes the handler, and then either writes the return value through a message converter or renders a view. A servlet filter runs before this flow and can reject the request first. A separately mapped servlet may handle another path. The front-controller idea is central coordination, not a claim of being the first code for every incoming packet.

sections.title: Request Flow Through DispatcherServlet
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A[HTTP Request] --> B[DispatcherServlet
front controller] B --> C[HandlerMapping
find controller method] C --> D[HandlerAdapter
invoke method] D --> E[Controller method runs] E --> F[HttpMessageConverter
object to JSON] F --> G[HTTP Response] ```

sections.title: DispatcherServlet in Action with Spring Boot
When DispatcherServlet Comes Into Play
sections.content:
You rely on DispatcherServlet whenever you build a **Spring MVC REST API or web application**. If you're using Spring Boot with spring-boot-starter-web, it's already there — you don't configure it manually.

Use DispatcherServlet when you need **centralized request handling** with Spring's ecosystem: dependency injection in controllers, declarative validation with @Valid, AOP-based transaction management, or HandlerInterceptors for cross-cutting concerns. If you're building a pure servlet-based app without Spring, you'd write individual servlets per endpoint. But in Spring MVC, DispatcherServlet handles routing for all endpoints through a single entry point.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking controllers are servlets**: Freshers often believe each @RestController is a servlet that directly receives HTTP requests. In reality, controllers are plain Spring beans — DispatcherServlet is the only servlet, and it delegates to controllers.
- **Not understanding why URL patterns matter**: If you manually register DispatcherServlet with pattern `/api/*`, requests to `/health` won't reach it. Spring Boot registers it at `/` so all requests go through it.
- **Assuming DispatcherServlet does business logic**: It's purely a coordinator — it routes requests, invokes handlers, and formats responses, but never contains your domain logic.

question: What is ViewResolver in Spring MVC?
title: ViewResolver in Spring MVC — Resolving View Names to Templates
direct_answer: A ViewResolver turns a logical view name returned by a view-oriented @Controller into a View implementation. An InternalResourceViewResolver can map users to /WEB-INF/views/users.jsp; a Thymeleaf resolver can map it to a template. Response-body methods normally use HttpMessageConverters instead, although Spring MVC can be configured with other view/negotiation arrangements.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how traditional @Controller view resolution works for server-side HTML rendering
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking ViewResolver is used in REST APIs — it's only for @Controller methods returning view names, not @RestController returning JSON
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention ContentNegotiatingViewResolver for multiple view types, and explain that @RestController bypasses ViewResolver entirely because @ResponseBody is implicit

sections.title: How a ViewResolver Maps a Logical View Name
sections.content:
ViewResolver does not always mean an HTML file. Spring has view abstractions for redirects, feeds, documents, and custom rendering, and multiple resolvers can be ordered. ContentNegotiatingViewResolver coordinates candidate views based on requested media types but does not itself render content.

Keep API controllers and page controllers clear enough that a String return value is not ambiguous to readers.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Controller returns a logical name and adds attributes to Model.
One or more ViewResolvers find a suitable View.
The View renders with the model into the response.
@ResponseBody/@RestController bypasses ordinary view-name resolution for body return values.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A method can add model.addAttribute("users", users) and return "users". The resolver supplies the physical template and the view renders it. The exact prefix/suffix belongs to the selected view technology and configuration. Returning the literal String from a @RestController instead writes it as body text; it does not resolve the template.

sections.title: ViewResolver at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|@Controller path|~Returns a view name|"users" is logical|ViewResolver finds the file|server-side HTML
blue|InternalResourceViewResolver|~JSP rendering|prefix + suffix|/WEB-INF/views/users.jsp|classic stack
emerald|ThymeleafViewResolver|~Spring Boot default|looks in templates/|templates/users.html|modern engine
rose|@RestController bypass|~No view resolution|@ResponseBody implicit|object to JSON directly|ViewResolver never runs

sections.title: Traditional MVC Controller with ViewResolver
When ViewResolver Matters in Real Projects
sections.content: Use ViewResolver when you're building **server-side rendered web applications** where the backend generates HTML pages. Typical scenarios: (1) Admin dashboards or internal tools where SEO and JavaScript frameworks aren't priorities — Spring MVC with Thymeleaf is faster to develop than a separate React frontend. (2) Multi-page applications (MPAs) where each route renders a full page refresh, common in enterprise intranets. (3) Form-heavy workflows like checkout flows or wizards where you want server-side validation and rendering. Do NOT use ViewResolver in REST APIs. If your controller methods return JSON to a React or Angular frontend, you need @RestController, not @Controller with views.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @Controller instead of @RestController for REST APIs**: Freshers add ViewResolver config to a REST API project, then wonder why they get 404 errors. If you're returning JSON, use @RestController which has implicit @ResponseBody on every method — ViewResolver is never called.
- **Forgetting template files in the classpath**: You configure ThymeleafViewResolver but put templates in src/main/webapp instead of src/main/resources/templates. Spring Boot's default resolver looks in classpath:templates/, not webapp.
- **Returning view names from @RestController methods**: If you accidentally use @RestController and return a String, Spring treats it as the response body (literal string), not a view name. You'll see "userList" as plain text in the browser instead of rendered HTML.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: ViewResolver is used in traditional Spring MVC apps where @Controller methods return view names. When your method returns the string 'users', DispatcherServlet hands that string to ViewResolver to find the matching template.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: ThymeleafViewResolver: the Spring Boot default when Thymeleaf is on the classpath. Looks for templates/users.html.
InternalResourceViewResolver: the JSP approach. Adds a prefix and suffix to construct the file path.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: ViewResolver decouples controller code from template locations. Your controller just returns a logical name. The resolver handles where the file actually lives and which template engine renders it.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: candidates miss: @RestController bypasses ViewResolver entirely. The return object goes directly to HttpMessageConverter. ViewResolver is only in the path when you use @Controller returning a view name string — not in any REST API code.

speakable_v2.cap: If you're building REST APIs you'll never touch ViewResolver. It only matters for server-rendered Thymeleaf or JSP pages.

question: What is HandlerMapping in Spring MVC?
title: HandlerMapping in Spring MVC — URL to Controller Method Resolution
direct_answer: `HandlerMapping` is the Spring MVC strategy that finds a handler for an incoming request. For annotated controllers, `RequestMappingHandlerMapping` registers `@RequestMapping`, `@GetMapping`, and similar methods at startup, then matches requests by their mapping conditions and returns the handler together with applicable interceptors.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of Spring MVC internal knowledge beyond just writing @GetMapping annotations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing HandlerMapping exists — thinking Spring magically routes requests without understanding the lookup mechanism
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention multiple HandlerMapping beans can exist with different priorities, and Spring tries them in order until one returns a handler

sections.title: The Request Router in Spring MVC
sections.content:
**HandlerMapping** is the component responsible for finding which controller method (handler) should process an incoming HTTP request. Imagine you send a GET request to `/api/users/42`.

DispatcherServlet receives it and asks HandlerMapping: "Which method handles this?" HandlerMapping scans all registered controller methods, checks their **@RequestMapping** annotations (or shortcuts like @GetMapping), and returns the matching method. The most common implementation is **RequestMappingHandlerMapping**, which Spring Boot configures automatically. It builds an internal map during startup: URL pattern + HTTP method → controller method. When a request arrives, it performs a fast lookup in this map. HandlerMapping doesn't invoke the method — it just returns a **HandlerExecutionChain** (the matched method plus any interceptors) back to DispatcherServlet. This separation of concerns keeps routing logic isolated from execution logic. Multiple HandlerMapping beans can coexist with different **order priorities**, so Spring tries them sequentially until one returns a handler.

sections.title: HandlerMapping at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|RequestMappingHandlerMapping|~Default implementation|scans @RequestMapping|builds URL to method map|runs at startup
blue|Runtime lookup|~Per request|matches path + HTTP method|returns HandlerExecutionChain|includes interceptors
emerald|Multiple mappings|~Ordered by priority|controllers + static resources|tried in sequence|first match wins
rose|Ambiguous mapping|~Two identical patterns|fails fast at startup|AmbiguousMappingException|fix duplicate routes

sections.title: How HandlerMapping Resolves Controller Methods
When HandlerMapping Matters
sections.content: You interact with HandlerMapping indirectly every time you write **@GetMapping, @PostMapping, or @RequestMapping** — those annotations tell RequestMappingHandlerMapping how to route requests. You'd explicitly configure custom HandlerMapping beans when building **non-standard routing logic**: routing based on custom headers, versioning APIs through Accept headers (Accept: application/vnd.company.v2+json), or serving static resources through ResourceHandlerMapping. In most Spring Boot REST APIs, the default RequestMappingHandlerMapping handles everything. But understanding it helps debug routing conflicts — like two methods with overlapping patterns — because HandlerMapping throws AmbiguousMappingException when it can't decide.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing HandlerMapping exists**: Learners think Spring "just knows" which method to call. They don't realize DispatcherServlet delegates to HandlerMapping for this lookup. When routing breaks, they don't know where to look.
- **Assuming only one HandlerMapping**: Spring registers several by default — RequestMappingHandlerMapping for controllers, SimpleUrlHandlerMapping for static resources. If you register a custom one without setting order, it might not run.
- **Conflicting mappings without realizing**: Writing two methods with @GetMapping("/users/{id}") and @GetMapping("/users/{name}") causes AmbiguousMappingException at startup because HandlerMapping can't distinguish them — Learners think "oh, one's an id, one's a name" but HandlerMapping sees identical patterns.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Routing Responsibility**: HandlerMapping's only job is finding which controller method matches an incoming request — it doesn't invoke the method or process the response
**RequestMappingHandlerMapping**: The default implementation that scans @RequestMapping, @GetMapping, @PostMapping annotations and builds an internal routing map at startup
**Multiple HandlerMappings**: Spring can have several HandlerMapping beans with different order values — DispatcherServlet tries them sequentially until one returns a match
**HandlerExecutionChain**: HandlerMapping returns this object containing the matched handler method plus any HandlerInterceptors that apply to it
**Pattern Matching**: Supports path variables like /users/{id}, wildcards like /docs/**, and HTTP method filtering — all configured through annotation attributes

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`HandlerMapping` is the routing strategy used by Spring MVC's `DispatcherServlet`. For annotated controllers, `RequestMappingHandlerMapping` detects methods marked with `@RequestMapping`, `@GetMapping`, and related annotations during startup. It registers the complete conditions for each method, including path, HTTP method, parameters, headers, and media types.

Suppose a controller declares `@GetMapping("/users/{id}")`. When `GET /users/42` arrives, `DispatcherServlet` checks its ordered HandlerMapping objects. The matching mapping returns a `HandlerExecutionChain` containing that controller method and any interceptors. A `HandlerAdapter` then resolves arguments such as `id` and invokes the method.

A missing match normally ends as 404 before controller code runs. Two methods with the same effective conditions cannot both be registered, so startup fails with an ambiguous-mapping error. The names `{id}` and `{name}` alone do not make two path patterns different.

speakable_v2.hook: HandlerMapping is the routing table inside Spring MVC — it's what turns a URL into a specific controller method.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: HandlerMapping is the Spring MVC component that decides which controller method handles a given request. When DispatcherServlet receives GET /api/users/1, it asks HandlerMapping: which method owns this?

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: At startup, RequestMappingHandlerMapping — the default implementation — scans all your @Controller and @RestController beans, reads their @GetMapping, @PostMapping, and related annotations, and builds a lookup table. Every incoming request hits this table.

beats.label: example
beats.content: The result isn't just a method reference. HandlerMapping returns a HandlerExecutionChain — the controller method plus any interceptors that apply to this URL pattern. Interceptors are attached at the HandlerMapping level.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: If two controller methods register the same effective request conditions, Spring rejects the ambiguous mapping while the application context starts. Variable names such as `{id}` and `{name}` do not distinguish otherwise identical patterns.

speakable_v2.cap: HandlerMapping is built once at startup. If your URL doesn't match any registered handler, you get 404 — Spring never reaches a controller.

question: What happens when a Spring Boot application starts with Spring MVC?
title: Spring MVC Auto-Configuration at Startup — What Spring Boot Does
direct_answer: When a servlet web application has Spring MVC on the classpath and no conflicting user configuration, Spring Boot auto-configures the DispatcherServlet and MVC infrastructure. Spring itself detects @Controller beans and builds request mappings. Message converters and view resolvers are added conditionally from the libraries and beans present; Jackson or Thymeleaf is not guaranteed unless its support is on the classpath.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring Boot auto-configuration for Spring MVC and what happens behind the scenes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing why adding spring-boot-starter-web is sufficient to get a working REST API — magic is auto-configuration
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention WebMvcAutoConfiguration class and how adding @EnableWebMvc disables auto-configuration, forcing manual configuration

sections.title: What Spring Boot Adds Around Spring MVC
sections.content:
Auto-configuration is assembled from small conditional configurations rather than one fixed list. The conditions look at the application type, classpath, properties, and existing beans.

The mapping registry is built from actual controller beans; Boot does not independently scan 'all controllers' as a separate magic step. Default exception resolvers cover framework exceptions, while Boot's error endpoint provides a fallback error response when an error reaches the container. Application-specific error contracts still need deliberate exception handling.

**Example.** With starter-web and no replacement MVC configuration, Boot registers MVC infrastructure, message converters, static-resource handling, and DispatcherServlet-related setup. Adding a custom ObjectMapper bean can refine JSON behavior without rebuilding all of MVC.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Boot registers servlet-web infrastructure when its conditions match.
RequestMappingHandlerMapping discovers mapped methods on controller beans.
Converters depend on available libraries and custom configuration.
Template view resolvers are conditional; a REST-only app may not have one.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: With spring-boot-starter-web, Boot normally creates the servlet application context, registers DispatcherServlet, and applies MVC defaults. RequestMappingHandlerMapping inspects controller beans after they are registered. If Jackson is available, MVC can write JSON. If Thymeleaf is also installed, its view resolver can render templates. User-defined beans and @EnableWebMvc can replace or change parts of these defaults, so the startup story should always mention conditions and back-off.

sections.title: Spring Boot MVC Startup Sequence
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A[main starts
SpringApplication.run] --> B[Application context boots] B --> C[WebMvcAutoConfiguration] C --> D[Register DispatcherServlet at /] D --> E[Scan @Controller beans
build HandlerMapping] E --> F[Register Jackson converter] F --> G[Embedded Tomcat on 8080
ready for requests] ```

sections.title: Minimal Spring Boot REST API with Auto-Configuration
When Auto-Configuration Applies
sections.content:
Spring Boot's MVC auto-configuration applies whenever you include **spring-boot-starter-web** in your dependencies and don't use **@EnableWebMvc** annotation. This covers most modern Spring Boot REST APIs and web apps.

Use it when you want **rapid development** without boilerplate configuration — building microservices, internal APIs, admin dashboards, or prototypes. Auto-configuration handles the 90% use case: JSON REST APIs with Jackson, embedded servlet containers, static resource serving, and basic error handling. If you need **custom MVC configuration** like adding interceptors, custom message converters, or CORS settings, you can still keep auto-configuration — just implement **WebMvcConfigurer** interface in a @Configuration class. Only disable auto-configuration (by adding @EnableWebMvc) when you need **full manual control**, which is rare in modern Spring Boot apps.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not understanding why it works**: Freshers add spring-boot-starter-web and write a controller — it works, but they don't know DispatcherServlet, HandlerMapping, and Jackson were auto-configured. This bites them when troubleshooting.
- **Adding @EnableWebMvc accidentally**: This annotation disables Spring Boot's auto-configuration, forcing you to manually configure everything. Freshers copy it from old Spring tutorials and wonder why their app breaks.
- **Assuming manual beans override auto-config**: If you define your own ObjectMapper bean, Spring Boot's auto-configured one backs off. Freshers don't realize this and create duplicate beans without understanding the conditional logic.
- **Not checking auto-configuration report**: Running with --debug flag shows which auto-configurations applied — freshers never look at this when debugging configuration issues.

What does @EnableWebMvc do and when should you avoid it?

speakable_v2.cap: WebMvcConfigurer is the right extension point for customizations. @EnableWebMvc is a full takeover — only use it if you mean it.

question: What is a HandlerInterceptor in Spring MVC?
title: HandlerInterceptor in Spring MVC — Pre and Post Processing
direct_answer: A HandlerInterceptor runs around Spring MVC handler execution. preHandle runs before the handler, postHandle after a successful handler invocation but before view completion, and afterCompletion after request completion. It is not simply Spring's equivalent of a servlet Filter: filters operate at the servlet-container level and can wrap request/response bodies, while interceptors know the selected handler.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Spring MVC's interceptor mechanism for cross-cutting concerns and how it differs from servlet filters
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Spring HandlerInterceptor with Servlet Filter — both intercept requests but at different layers with different capabilities
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the three methods: preHandle runs before controller, postHandle runs after controller but before response, afterCompletion runs after response is sent

sections.title: HandlerInterceptor in the MVC Pipeline
sections.content:
The callbacks do not all have identical guarantees. postHandle is not called when the handler throws before returning, while afterCompletion is intended for cleanup after MVC finishes and receives an exception when available. With asynchronous requests there are additional lifecycle callbacks.

Register interceptors through WebMvcConfigurer and specify path patterns carefully. Do not implement authorization ad hoc when Spring Security can express it consistently before controller execution.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Interceptor: MVC-aware and can inspect the HandlerMethod.
Filter: servlet-level, runs before DispatcherServlet, and can wrap bodies.
Use interceptors for handler-aware timing, locale, or request policy checks.
Authentication is normally handled by Spring Security's filter chain rather than custom interceptor code.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: An interceptor can record a start time in preHandle and attach handler information to a timing metric in afterCompletion. Returning false from preHandle stops handler execution, but the interceptor must then complete the response if needed. Filters are a better fit for compression, raw request wrapping, and concerns that apply outside MVC. Rate limiting and security may require filters or dedicated infrastructure depending on where the protection must run.

sections.title: HandlerInterceptor Lifecycle
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A[Request] --> B[preHandle] B -->|returns true| C[Controller method] B -->|returns false| X[Request aborted] C --> D[postHandle] D --> E[Response written] E --> F[afterCompletion
always runs, even on exception] ```

sections.title: Implementing a Logging HandlerInterceptor
When to Use HandlerInterceptor vs Servlet Filter
sections.content:
Use **HandlerInterceptor** when you need **Spring-specific features**: access to the matched controller method (handler object), dependency injection of Spring beans, or modification of ModelAndView in traditional MVC apps. Best for **authentication/authorization** (you know which method is about to run, can check method-level @Secured annotations), **request logging** with controller context, **tenant or locale resolution** (need to set data in Spring's context for controllers to use).

Use **Servlet Filter** for **lower-level concerns** that must apply even to static resources or non-Spring endpoints: CORS headers (need to set headers before Spring MVC runs), compression, encoding, or security filters that inspect raw request bytes. Filters see every request; HandlerInterceptors only run for requests that match a controller. In practice, most Spring Boot apps use HandlerInterceptors for business concerns and rely on Spring Security's filters for authentication, because Security integrates with the filter chain directly.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing with Servlet Filters**: Freshers hear "intercepts requests" and think it's the same as Filter. But HandlerInterceptor runs after DispatcherServlet resolves the handler — so it has access to the controller method and Spring context. Filters run before DispatcherServlet even sees the request.
- **Returning false in preHandle without setting response**: If preHandle returns false, Spring short-circuits — the controller doesn't run. Freshers forget to write an error response, so the client gets an empty 200 OK.
- **Assuming postHandle runs on exception**: If the controller throws an exception, postHandle is skipped. Only afterCompletion runs, and it receives the exception as a parameter.
- **Not registering the interceptor**: Writing a HandlerInterceptor class but forgetting to add it to InterceptorRegistry means it never runs — freshers wonder why their logging doesn't work.

seo.metaDescription: Learn HandlerInterceptor in Spring MVC — preHandle, postHandle, afterCompletion methods, difference from Servlet Filter, and registration with WebMvcConfigurer.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: HandlerInterceptor and Servlet Filter both intercept requests — but they live at different layers and see different things.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: A Servlet Filter runs at the servlet container level, before DispatcherServlet even sees the request. It has no access to the Spring context and doesn't know which controller will handle the request.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: A HandlerInterceptor runs inside the Spring MVC layer, after DispatcherServlet has identified the handler. It has full access to the Spring context and knows which controller method is about to be called.

beats.label: differences
content: preHandle: runs before the controller method. Return false to abort the request entirely.
postHandle: runs after the controller method but before the response is written. Can modify ModelAndView.
afterCompletion: runs after the complete response, even if an exception was thrown. Good for cleanup and timing.

beats.label: when_to_pick
beats.content: Use a Filter for concerns that apply regardless of Spring — encoding, security at the container level. Use HandlerInterceptor when you need Spring beans injected or need to know which controller is running — logging, role-based access checks against your user service.

beats.label: tiny_example
beats.content: non-obvious: postHandle is only called if the controller method succeeded. If the method throws an exception, postHandle is skipped. afterCompletion is always called — that's the right place for guaranteed cleanup.

speakable_v2.cap: Register interceptors through WebMvcConfigurer.addInterceptors — you can also restrict them to specific URL patterns with addPathPatterns.

question: What is HttpMessageConverter in Spring MVC?
title: HttpMessageConverter in Spring — Serialization and Deserialization
direct_answer: HttpMessageConverter reads a supported HTTP body into a controller argument and writes a return value to a response body. Spring selects a converter from the Java type, request Content-Type, response Accept choices, declared consumes/produces conditions, and registered converter capabilities. @RequestBody and @ResponseBody participate; methods with no body do not necessarily use a converter.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how @RequestBody and @ResponseBody actually work under the hood
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Jackson just works magically without understanding the MessageConverter chain and content negotiation

sections.title: How HttpMessageConverter Bridges HTTP Bodies and Java Values
sections.content: Controllers usually let MVC call converters, but manually using ObjectMapper is legitimate in lower-level transformations, custom converters, tests, or special payload processing. The rule is to avoid duplicating normal MVC serialization in each controller, not to ban ObjectMapper. Adding an XML library also requires a compatible converter and model; one particular dependency does not configure every XML path.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Jackson JSON support comes from a Jackson converter when its dependencies/configuration are present.
Content-Type guides reading; Accept and produces guide writing.
406 means no acceptable writable representation; 415 means the request representation is unsupported.
XML can be provided by different XML converters; jackson-dataformat-xml is not the only possible mechanism.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For example, a POST with Content-Type application/json can be read by MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter into CreateOrderRequest. Returning OrderResponse can be written by the same converter as application/json when the client accepts it. A plain byte array, Resource, String, or form body may use a different converter.

sections.title: HttpMessageConverter at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Serialization|~Java object to body|@ResponseBody return|MappingJackson2 writes JSON|outgoing response
blue|Deserialization|~Body to Java object|@RequestBody parameter|Jackson reads JSON|incoming request
emerald|Content negotiation|~Picks the converter|Accept header for write|Content-Type for read|first match wins
rose|No matching converter|~Media type unsupported|returns 406|add jackson-dataformat-xml for XML|JSON works by default

sections.title: Using HttpMessageConverter with @RequestBody and @ResponseBody
When HttpMessageConverter Is Active in Your API
sections.content: HttpMessageConverter is used automatically in every **@RestController** method with @RequestBody or @ResponseBody (which is implicit in @RestController). Concrete scenarios: (1) Building a REST API where Angular or React frontend sends JSON to your backend — the converter deserializes the request body into your DTO. (2) Microservice communication using RestTemplate or WebClient — when you call restTemplate.postForObject(), the converter serializes your request object to JSON. (3) Content negotiation scenarios where the same endpoint can return JSON or XML depending on the Accept header — Spring selects the appropriate converter. (4) Custom serialization needs like excluding null fields or formatting dates — you configure the ObjectMapper bean that MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter uses. You don't manually invoke converters in your code. Spring's DispatcherServlet and RequestMappingHandlerAdapter handle it transparently based on annotations.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting Jackson dependency in non-Boot projects**: Freshers expect JSON to work without adding Jackson to pom.xml. Spring Boot includes it by default, but plain Spring MVC doesn't. Without a JSON converter, you get 406 Not Acceptable errors.
- **Not understanding Content-Type vs Accept headers**: They send JSON but forget Content-Type: application/json header, so Spring can't find a converter to read the request body. Or they expect JSON response but the Accept header says text/html, so Spring picks StringHttpMessageConverter instead.
- **Returning raw List from @RestController**: Returning List<User> works because MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter handles collections, but freshers think they need to manually convert it to JSON string first. Never call ObjectMapper yourself in a controller — the converter does it.
- **Assuming XML support exists by default**: Jackson handles JSON automatically in Boot, but XML requires adding jackson-dataformat-xml dependency. Without it, clients requesting application/xml get 406 errors.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
speakable_v2.hook: When you return a Java object from a @RestController, something has to turn it into JSON bytes. That something is HttpMessageConverter.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: HttpMessageConverter handles both directions: it reads incoming request bodies and writes outgoing response bodies. For JSON, the default converter is MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter, auto-configured when Jackson is on the classpath.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: Spring selects the right converter using content negotiation. For writing a response, it checks the Accept header the client sent. For reading a request body, it checks the Content-Type header. If you send JSON with Content-Type application/json, Spring uses Jackson to deserialize it into your @RequestBody parameter.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter: handles JSON. Auto-configured. Used for most REST APIs.
StringHttpMessageConverter: for String return types, produces text/plain.
ByteArrayHttpMessageConverter: for binary data like file downloads.
Jaxb2RootElementHttpMessageConverter handles supported JAXB-bound XML types; Jackson XML uses MappingJackson2XmlHttpMessageConverter when its module is configured.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: gotcha: If a client sends Accept: application/xml but you only have the JSON converter configured, Spring returns 406 Not Acceptable — not a serialization error. The converter chain is checked before your method return value is touched.

speakable_v2.cap: Customize Jackson by defining an ObjectMapper bean — Spring Boot will use yours instead of the default configuration.
